eyebrow: Statistics & Probability for Data Science · Chapter 5, Lesson 24
subtitle: Is the mix of categories different from what chance alone would produce?

caption: Close to expected -> small statistic. Diverges -> large. Degrees of freedom set the p-value.

code:
obs = np.array([70, 55, 50, 58, 67])   # tickets per weekday, 60 expected
res = stats.chisquare(obs)
print(round(res.statistic,3), round(res.pvalue,4))
# 4.633  0.327
caption: Day-to-day variation is entirely plausible under an even workload -- not proof it's perfectly even.

code:
table = pd.DataFrame({"bought": [120,95,60], "no_purchase": [880,605,240]},
                     index=["mobile","desktop","tablet"])
chi2, p, dof, expected = stats.chi2_contingency(table)
print(round(chi2,3), round(p,4), dof)
# 12.483  0.0019  2
caption: H0: purchase rate is the same across devices. p=0.0019 makes independence look implausible.

code:
r = table["bought"] / table.sum(axis=1)
print(r.round(3))
# mobile 0.120  desktop 0.136  tablet 0.200

# expected tablet "bought": 41.2  --  observed: 60
caption: A significant chi-square says "somewhere" -- standardized residuals pin it to tablet (~2.9).

code:
n = table.values.sum()
k = min(table.shape) - 1
v = np.sqrt(chi2 / (n * k))
print(round(v, 3))   # 0.079 -- a SMALL association
caption: Significance isn't magnitude: real difference exists, but device explains little of who buys.
